utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in -- in and around the courtroom, and in Osijek. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Case Manager Thomas Laugel, legal intern Mirela Bogdanovic Nikcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the parties have been told that there is a problem with the videolink and more particularly an encrypting issue. That means that we can't go into private session with Osijek. Now my question is: Do you have anything in private session in chief and in cross? Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. There's no expectation of such a need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's solved, then. The only thing we need to do, then, is to be very careful about eventually redactions because redactions should be asked for in private session and we can't go into private session. So please be careful. The witness may -- the witness is already in, of course. Good morning to you, Madam Registrar, in Osijek. Mr. Stringer. Oh, sorry. I, of course, have to ask for the solemn declaration. The witness has no protective measures. Good morning -- good morning, Mr. Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand? Good morning, Mr. Witness. Thank you for coming to Osijek to assist the Tribunal. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't have translation of what the witness says. Mr. Witness, could you -- could you say "test, test"? Oh, that's not very useful. We need something to be translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you -- thank you very much. Mr. Witness, could you please tell us your name and your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ljubo Pribudic; 5th of April, 1940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to make the solemn declaration, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that by doing so, you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Could I ask you to read the solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This sound from Osijek is very bad. We couldn't hear the last part of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please repeat the declaration. There was a problem with the sound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, this is Doug Stringer in the courtroom in The Hague. Can you see me and understand me?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I can see you very well, and I hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, where did you live in 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: In 1991, I lived in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And at that time, were you married? Did you have a family?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Married, wife, four children, and me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How old were you then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I'm 73 now, and in 1991, I would have been, what, 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And back in 1991, Mr. Pribudic, how were you employed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I was a craftsman. I had my own private work-shop, ever since 1963. I had my own work-shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What kind of craft did you practice?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I had a work-shop for repairing, mounting, and maintenance of all sorts of weighing scales.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And did your work on the scales take you to other parts of what was then Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went everywhere; Macedonia, Slovenia, all of Croatia. Wherever they called me, I went there. And I had a very good reputation because we worked honestly and fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you know Goran Hadzic before the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Had you ever seen him or had you ever heard anything about Mr. Hadzic before the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: But his director at Pacetin was the director of the kombinat, Mladen Brkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you say that name again, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Mladen Mrkic, M-r-k-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: He was the director of Kooperacija. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you did know him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you said - I'm just looking at our transcript - that his director was the director of kombinat. Who was Mr. Mrkic the director of?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkic was the director of Mr. Hadzic and all co-operatives around Vukovar, such as at Trpinja, Pacetin, and other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Pribudic, during the months of autumn 1991, did you participate in the defence of Vukovar as a fighter or as a defender?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges, please, in just a few words what you did.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Where? When? During the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. In what way did you contribute to the defence.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I worked at the staff. I took food to the people who were in basements. I guarded places at night. And I was in the basement of the former Hungarian school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Where was your family during that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: My family was partly in Germany, and my wife was with me. And my daughters were with their husbands, one was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you mentioned the basement of the former Hungarian school. Was that located close to your house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: It was two houses away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges the name --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, I was in my own basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What street was your house and the Hungarian school located on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Stjepana Radica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: About how far away was that from the hospital in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: A kilometre. And the hospital is still at the same place. And the house is still there, but now it's a police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, could you please tell the Judges what happened then on the 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Vukovar fell and then the army moved in. We were almost out of food already, and then the army lined up everyone on the street and took us to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How many people were in your group that was taken to Velepromet on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The sound is so bad that it's unintelligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, I'm sorry, but with the technical problem, we did not get your last answer. Could I just ask you to tell us how many people were in your group when you were taken to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but there were many people, perhaps as many as 500, or even more, counting the women and children too. There were many of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we'll talk about things that happened while you were at Velepromet. But could you first tell the Judges how many days or how many nights, then, did you spend in Velepromet before you were moved?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Three nights, the 18th, 19th, 20th. Yeah, three nights at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at Velepromet, where were you placed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: When we arrived at Velepromet we were separated, and I was put in the so-called room of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, I'd ask that Mr. Pribudic be provided with 65 ter 2802, which is an aerial image.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the entire building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, are you -- Mr. Pribudic --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: The white area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- let me just ask you a couple of questions. First of all, this photograph that you're looking at, do you recognise what this place is?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, let me ask you just to stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I don't know whether there's a problem with the volume, whether it might be better if the microphone was moved closer to him or not, whether that's an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, if I could just ask you to tell us, in general, what does this picture show?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is unintelligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm in your hands. I don't know what to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to get an image from Osijek, because that's generally -- generally one can see whether it works or not, the videolink, I mean. But obviously we don't get an image. Oh, there it is. Try once again, Mr. Stringer. I think we are back in business.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, on this photograph, do you see the location of the room of death that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I think it must be here, on this side. Here, this is the carpentry, and these are the hangars made of -- they're made of sheet metal. They were called the tin cans. This is the Velepromet yard. Only I don't know what the white -- this thing here in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I ask to you take a pen or a marker and to place a circle around the area of the room of death.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: This is the entrance. This is that building where ... this is the auxiliary building. I don't know what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If -- with the Registrar's assistance, perhaps, if we could just be shown the photograph, we can get an idea roughly of the location that's been marked. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, during the time that you were in the room of death on the 18th, can you tell the Judges what happened, in general? What was taking place and what were the conditions like in there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: The conditions were catastrophical. The number of people increased from minute to minute. And it's hard to say, but there must have been more than 200 of us inside. It was unbearable. And that was how it was until midnight. After midnight, they started taking people out, taking them taking them somewhere, but whoever was taken out was gone for good.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you ever able -- or at that time did you learn or -- or get any information about what was happening to those people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Nobody ever told me anything, but those guys never returned. And shots could be heard. Whenever someone was taken out, there was a shot or a burst of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you know someone in that room who was named Ivo, who worked as a carpenter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Ivo. Carpenter. There was a guy named Ivo, but he was a wood cutter. But I didn't know any carpenter by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At some --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a wood cutter by the name of Ivo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: What does that mean? He got killed. He was taken out and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him after he was killed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I saw him lying dead by the tracks of Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, on the next day, the 19th of November, were you moved to a different location?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: The 19th. Cvjeticanin moved me to the carpentry. It was in the same building. There was a hallway that divided the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And can you describe the situation there in the carpentry on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: In the carpentry on the 19th, there were mostly women. A couple of men. And when I entered, the women were taken out and taken away by buses. I and two more men stayed behind. During the night, women were arriving, and men too, but they didn't stay long.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the next day, the 20th of November, were you then -- at that time, in the morning, were you still in the carpentry?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, three men came in and first started beating me inside, and then they took me out and beat me unconscious. I had some money in my pockets, some German money. They took it all. They also took my coat and my stock -- stockings. I was unconscious outside. When I woke up before dawn, I saw that I was in the room of death. I was lying, and I looked at the man beside me. It was Zeljko Buljan. He said, Don't be afraid. I'm here too. And I stayed there until morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pribudic, you've indicated that when you woke up then after the beating, you were back in this room of death. In addition to Mr. Buljan, were there other people there that you -- that you knew?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: There was Drago Vertofer [phoen]. There was Ivo Vidaj, Jozo Sidl. Ferhan Perkovic, we called him Little Perkan at school. He was also taken out and killed. And on the second day or the second night, they crammed 18 of us on a bus and took us to Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pribudic, before you were taken to Mitrovica, were you and the others taken to a different location first?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: No, not then. To Negoslavci and there we waited about an hour to be admitted. And then from Negoslavci to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Witness. Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but I believe there might be a transcription mistake there at line 23, as far as the name that was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, you were giving us the names of some of the other people who were in that room of death. You mentioned a Drago. What was his family name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Verkofer [phoen]. Dragutin Verkofer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How were you transported to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: By bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And where in Vukovar were you placed on the buses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: We boarded the buses at the barracks. First, we were taken there. And when we arrived at the barracks, hungry and thirsty, they gave us bread and water and canned food and cigarettes. I don't smoke but another man, Vlado, said to me, Take some for me too. And I was surprised. I was very thirsty. I emptied an entire pitcher of water. And around 7.00 in the morning, we were put on buses where we stayed until 9.00 and then we were taken to Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, are you able to recall the date then that you were taken to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: The date. Was it the 20th or the 21st? It was the 21st, at dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what was your condition? You mentioned that you had been beaten while at Velepromet. What was your condition at the time that you were being transported to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I was all beaten up. My head was bashed in. When we reached Buljani, I woke up and I saw blood running down my face. I saw that there was a lid next to a bucket where -- that we used to relieve ourselves, so I took the lid --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat what he said then. The interpreters didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to tell us again what you did with the lid that you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: The lid was actually a lid of a large tin that they provided us with to relieve ourselves in. I don't know if it was clean or not, but at any rate, it was wet. I broke it in half and then bent it again, and I used it as a stitch, in fact, to stitch up the wound in my head, and that's how I kept it then throughout the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges what happened when you and the others arrived at Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in Mitrovica, we stood there in the centre for quite a long time. I think more than two hours. There were individuals boarding the bus, but they didn't take us out. They had batons that they hit us with on our shoulders and our heads. When we reached the KP Dom at Mitrovica, they took us out into a basketball court. It was a concrete surface and they told us to lie prone on it. There was pouring rain. We lay there for quite a long time. Then they told us, Get up. And they forced us to run a gauntlet. There were was a fence there and there were two lines of people, and you had to run as fast as your feet carried you, otherwise you would get so many blows that you would fall down and not be able to get up. I received a blow to my head by a baton. I was knocked off my feet but I managed to get up and run the gauntlet to the end. Then we reached a patch of green. They told us that we should sit down and take our shoes off. Then they started beating us by giving us blows to our soles, the soles of our feet, and kept on hitting us all the way up our body. I must tell you that it's unbearable pain to be hit around your knees. One of the men fainted. It was the little Soljic. Then they told us to get up and approach a building there. I think it's number -- building number one, if I recall correctly. There was rain and a culvert that was full of running water. They told us to lie prone and put our faces into the culvert. Now, we, of course, had to lift our heads from time to time because we couldn't bear staying under water. One of them said, Captain comrade, referring to one of us, this one is not moving. He's finished. He is as dead as a doornail. And then he told him, Dusko, okay, bring a truck over to gate 1. And I thought, we're done for now. As the truck came, they told us that we should go into the building in threes. They asked me to carry Veber, the one who couldn't get up, and as we got in -- upstairs into the room, I fell asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You mentioned someone named Soljic, I believe little Soljic. Do you know what became of him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Little Soljic. He died. He died.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, after you were inside, could you tell the Judges about the room or the rooms where you and other prisoners were held.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: In Mitrovica, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: What was it like. Well, it was a room. The heating was on, and I suppose they did it on purpose. It was winter time. They opened windows that were high up, overhead, so you had this cold air coming from up -- from up there. And then it was very hot as well. It was the first building, I think, and they laid it out with an asphalt surface. So we were lying down on it, rolling on it, like pigs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were there any beds in this room?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Not in the first one, no. There were blankets on the floor, and we were lying one next to the other. When we went to the fourth room, which was at the end of the the corridor, there you had very narrow bunk beds. I was lying on the bed below.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in this first room you've described, approximately how many prisoners were there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: At least 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: We were lying cheek by jaw, like sardines. If you had to go and relieve yourself at night, you had to step over someone and then you would fall over them. It was a sea of human bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the other room that you described that had the beds, approximately how many people were in that room?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: All the rooms were overcrowded. Not just the one where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you describe the uniforms worn by the guards who were working at the prison and who participated in beatings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: The uniforms --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's compound and leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, he's just talked about some beatings, I believed. We'll go back to it. I apologise for the compound question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, you described a beating that occurred upon your arrival. Do you recall what types of uniforms they were wearing? The people who were giving you the beating.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Those who received us were wearing blue uniforms. I don't know if they were also the ones beating us. I didn't dare raise my head. But I think they had blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then during the time that you were being held in the rooms and -- and were otherwise there, what, in general, did the guards wear?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: The guards who came wore olive-drab camouflage uniforms. Some of them also had white belt -- belts, and we surmised that they were policemen, and they were mostly Montenegrins. But they had olive-drab uniforms, the uniforms of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were there any other times when groups were taken for beatings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: They took out one by one. I don't know what they did with each and every one of them. At any rate, some of them would come back black and blue. Others would come back crying. At any rate, none of those who returned had not been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you ever taken outside again for any beatings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I was taken out when Hadzic was beating me up. Other than that, they didn't take us -- take me out for beatings. They would take us out for interrogations with a general and a -- and another individual. I knew him. I knew the general from the army. And there was a major as well. And then I also received a -- a blow from a sergeant. So that was just that one blow. As for the general, he didn't beat me. He even offered me a shot of brandy. Since I was ill at the time, they did take me out. I had to rest my back against a wall and -- and spread my arms and stand like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned an encounter you had with Mr. Hadzic. Could you tell the Judges, please, as best as can you remember now when that happened? Was it in 1991 or ... after the 1st of the year, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: It all happened in 1991. I was released on the -- the 2nd of July. But they didn't beat me. Hadzic was the last one who beat me up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what happened when you met Mr. Hadzic there.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: What happened. How he beat me personally. He came to a room that was smaller, shorter than yours, but of the same breadth. He came and he says, Oh, there you are, Ljubo, the scalesman. He said -- I said yes. So he stepped toward a desk where there were three persons seated. One was called Stankovic and for the others, I'm not sure. Stankovic was in my group. I was a hunter, and I had my own group, and he was a member of my group at the time. Hadzic stepped toward the desk and they said, His dossier is fine. Because they were reading through all my particulars, first, last name, father, et cetera. And he turned back to me and said, Which side of the face did they slap you on? And I said, This one. And then he slapped me on the other side. And he said, Just so you're not beaten always on the same side. Then he stepped out of the room but he came back a minute later. And then he said to me, Does Mrkic owe you money? I said, No, but he did take -- I did loan him money but every time he paid back whenever he said that he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Pribudic, let me ask you there to just tell us, apart from yourself, were there any other prisoners present during this questioning, or this meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I was -- I was the only one in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall what Mr. Hadzic was wearing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: A camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You now just made a reference to someone named Mrkic. Is this the same person that you mentioned at the beginning of your evidence today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: It's the same Mrkic. His director. Because, on Fridays and Mondays, the four of us would meet up and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear because the line was very poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, we lost the very end of your -- of your sentence there. You say Mr. Mrkic was the director of Mr. Hadzic at his employment.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did -- you say Mr. Hadzic then stepped out of the room. Did he return?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Which gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Hadzic. He stepped out of the room and then went back in. I was under the impression that there was someone in the room next door who would be feeding him information. He would come back and then ask me, Where is your HDZ membership card? I replied, At Velepromet. He said, How come you have an HDZ membership card? You don't go much to the church. You're not a Communist. And then he turned back to leave when I replied, But I'm a Croat. And then he turned around dealt me a blow rather than a slap. And then -- what did he say? He -- yes, he swore at me, mentioning my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did the subject of your children come up?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: And then went back out. But then he would come back to the room again and ask me, Where are your sons? I told him, I don't know. They're in Germany. He asked, They're not over here. I replied, Goran, if they're here, then you should kill me and them. I said to that, I'll kill them both, and went out. This was very hard on me. My brain was thinking fast. And I was thinking what I should do. When he comes back, perhaps I should plan -- lunge for his neck and then try and strangle him. And then there was this man Ljubo holding a Kalashnikov. He trained it against me and threatened me, at which point Hadzic came to the room again. The man who was sitting at the desk told me, Ljubo, straighten up a bit. He realised that I would actually drop to the floor. So I stood up and Hadzic said to that, Who allowed you to stand up? The man at the desk said, I did. And then one of the four said, Gorane, it's been enough. And then the man who used to man the gate said, Take him out. And that was where my ordeal ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you told us earlier that you didn't -- you did not know Mr. Hadzic from before, so how did you know that this was him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: It was the four of the men who mentioned him. One of them was called Savic. And then there was this young lad as well, and the man carrying a Kalashnikov, as well as a person who used to be in the hangar. He was the one charged with the paperwork, with the dossier. He addressed him as Goran. And judging by his looks and his conduct, I concluded that it was him. But I didn't have an opportunity to see him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a person named Stankovic and you mentioned the hunting group. Do you know what his role was in this -- in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was his position, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He was a young man who had come to -- and joined my group several months previously. I would not have known that he was called Stankovic had it not been for my friend Cuk who said, Well, he's a young man, he's a judge, and he said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure if it was a judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he said, Well, why don't we let him join our group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, what was the -- did you learn what was the job or the position of Mr. Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: He asked me about a Hungarian and I said I don't know. And he told me then, Well, how come you don't know him? He is a hunter as well. And, well, I said, You're a hunter, I can't know them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, if you know or if you heard, what was the job or the position of Mr. Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I don't know. If he was a judge, then he must have gone through some schooling. There were about five or six of them coming that year. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Why do you say that he might -- he may have been a judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. Because that's not exactly what the witness said [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that he was a judge. Now was he or was he not, I don't know. Cuk told me that he was a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, how long, then, did you remain a prisoner at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: It was from the 7th of April, so from the 20th or the 21st up until the 7th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, after you were released, did you find your family?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I found them all in Zagreb. I came to Zagreb, and there I found my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us just briefly what had -- what had been her -- her path from Vukovar to Zagreb during the time that you were away.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: My wife left Vukovar from Velepromet by bus. She went from Velepromet to Sid where she spent the night, and she saw a note on the desk in Sid which said, If Ljubo, the scalesman, should come here, kill him right away. She saw that note. And then, what, the five of them went out. It was raining. There was a neighbour of ours, Danica. She said, You can come out. And she then went to Tuzla and somehow she found a bus that took her to Zagreb via Slavonski Brod. So that's it, in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges, please, Mr. Pribudic, what has been the impact of all these events on you and your family and your community in Vukovar in the years since?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: It was miserable. I didn't want to leave Vukovar because I thought who would do me any harm? Everybody knew me. I opened my shop to everyone, regardless of whether the person was a Croat, a Serb, or a Muslim. I respected every person. I loaned money to many. I had dealings with many people. People respected me. Many people were telling me, Ljubo, let's leave. And I had a truck available where I could have loaded some of my belongings and left, and I had money too. But I didn't leave. I was born a Dalmatian. I was born in Split; I have a flat there. And there I was a fool in Vukovar. So when I got to Velepromet, what did I find there? Sheer misery. They were people who were wretches.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. Mr. Gosnell, cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pribudic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Gosnell, and I represent Mr. Hadzic in these proceedings. I'll be asking you a few questions. If any of my questions appear to you unclear, please let me know and I'll do my best to assist you. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'd like to start with something that you just said a few minutes ago when you were asked the following question by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stringer. And the question was: "Now, you told us earlier that you didn't -- you did not know Mr. Hadzic from before, so how did you know that this was him?" And then your answer was: "It was the four of the men who mentioned him, one of them was called Savic. And then there was this young lad as well, and the man carrying a Kalashnikov, as well as a person who used to be in the hangar. He was the one charged with the paperwork, with the dossier. He addressed him as Goran. And judging by his looks and his conduct, I concluded that it was him. But I didn't have an opportunity to see him before." Do you remember giving that answer, Mr. Pribudic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So it's correct that you had not seen Mr. Hadzic before this occasion.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I said at the very beginning that I had seen him on the bridge, the Vuka bridge --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat. It was unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, could you please repeat that answer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I was on the Vuka bridge and Hadzic passed by, and I asked, Who is he? And they said, It's Hadzic. He's the warehouse keeper at Pacetin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I had no dealings with him. I worked -- I had some work on the Vuka bridge. It was -- it was in the 1970s.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could you please repeat, Mr. Pribudic, when you believe you saw him on the Vuka bridge.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: He was walking there. I didn't pay attention who he is -- who he was walking with. And he didn't accost me either. He just walked past.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pribudic, I know that it may be difficult with the videolink, hearing or understanding my questions, but I didn't ask you what he was doing or who he was with, or whether he spoke to you. My only question is: When did you see him on the Vuka bridge?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: When? Well, I don't remember the time. It was a man who didn't mean anything to me at the time. How should I remember? Anybody could have -- he could have been anybody. I didn't expect him, to remember, oh, now he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, we had a translation come through of your answer that said it was in the 1970s. Was the occasion that you saw Mr. Hadzic on the Vuka bridge several or many years before 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: How am I to know? I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, think back and try. Can you --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I wasn't waiting for Hadzic, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Witness. But think back, as best you can and --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: It was before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was it years before the war? Weeks? Months? A decade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Maybe two or three years before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was that the one and only occasion that you say you saw Mr. Hadzic before the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: That was the only occasion. I wouldn't even know if that colleague hadn't told me, That's Hadzic. I didn't care.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the man who came into the room to interrogate you at Sremska Mitrovica who you now testify was Goran Hadzic, would it be correct to say that you relied exclusively on what you were told or what was said by the other people in the room, and by that I mean that they referred to Goran Hadzic by name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I wasn't so attentive. He was beating me, slapping me every now and then, and I didn't ask, Who is the one slapping me? When I came to the room upstairs, then the hygiene inspector was -- he died recently at Kastela. I can't remember his name now. He was taken out immediately after me, and he said, Ljubo, that is Hadzic. And -- oh, now I remember his name, Emil Cakalic. But he didn't beat me, just interrogated me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well let me ask you this: If you can recall, when the man whom you later came to understand from Emil Cakalic was Goran Hadzic, when that man first entered the room where you were interrogated, did you recognise him as the man who had been identified to you on the Vuka bridge as Mr. Hadzic? Or not.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I recognised his head, his hair, beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that was on the basis and the strength of that one sighting on the Vuka bridge possibly years before.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I may have seen him a couple of times more, but I wasn't paying attention. I didn't look at everyone intently.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Okay. So now it's not true, it's not correct, then, what you said at line -- at page 19, when you testified to this Court when you said: "I didn't have an opportunity to see him before." As it turns out, you did, according to your testimony now, you did see him before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I wasn't paying attention, what I know, who I see. When you're not paying attention, you don't really know. You see dozens of people every day, but ... so what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you returned from the interrogation room, you've testified that you spoke to Emil Cakalic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry Mr. Gosnell. There -- the -- there was a question that you asked. It's at line 3 and following on page 25. Could you attempt to put that question to the witness again? The -- the question was: The man who came into the room to interrogate you at Sremska Mitrovica which, et cetera, would it be correct to say that you relied exclusively on what you were told or what was said by other people in that room? Could you attempt to put that question, that precise question again to the witness, please. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pribudic, I'll try to put this question slightly differently and hopefully it will be a bit easier to understand. At the moment when you were in the interrogation room, were you able to recognise him, the man who you say slapped you, on the basis of visually recognising him, or, rather, was it based on his name being mentioned by others in the room?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I recognised him because I had seen him. Those people weren't saying anything. The one who called him by name, Goran. I recognised him by sight, by his appearance. And then Cakalic also said, Yes, Ljubo, it's Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how did Mr. Cakalic know that you were talking about the same person?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I went upstairs and told him. And when he returned, he said, No, he didn't beat me. It is Hadzic, but he didn't beat me or anything. But I had been beaten before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how was it that Mr. Cakalic had seen Mr. Hadzic on this occasion, in order to be able to tell you, Yes, that's Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: But they took him out of that room downstairs where I was, and then he saw him. And when he returned, he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So are you saying that Mr. Cakalic also went and had an interrogation with Mr. Hadzic on this same day that you did?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the same day. The same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what did he tell you about that interrogation that he underwent?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I didn't ask him, nor did he volunteer any information. He only confirmed to me that it was -- it had been Hadzic there. But without my asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, at the time of this interrogation, were you in what you have described earlier as the big room that you were detained in? Is that where you were detained at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: All the rooms were big. Where I was, that was room 1. And then later I was in room 2, and later on, in room 4. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you remember which room were staying in at the time of this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was Dragutin Berghofer with you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Director Ivanisevic was there in the same room, Zvonko Ivanisevic. Then in that room there was - what's his name? - Danijel Rehak. But in a room where you go through such an ordeal, you can't remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was Dragutin Berghofer detained with you at Srebrenica while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry, you might want to correct that. I believe you said Srebrenica. At least that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Pribudic, my question was whether or not Dragutin Berghofer was detained with you at Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Detained at Sremska Mitrovica, yes, that's what he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In fact, you were taken --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: He stayed when I had already gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In fact, you and he travelled on the same bus from the JNA barracks on the 22nd of November to Sremska Mitrovica; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you had lived in Vukovar how many years before 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: From 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you lived near Dragutin Berghofer; correct? He was actually a neighbour of yours.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was four or five houses away from me. He had a work-shop for upholstery.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you recall whether he was in any of the same rooms as you were staying in at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Where he was? He was in the last room with me. He was with me as soon as we arrived, and then we went up to room 1 on the fourth floor. He was there too. And we were being beaten, and then he -- he freaked out, something clicked in his head from the beating. Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you say he was with you "as soon as we arrived, and then we went up to room 1 on the fourth floor." So am correct in understanding that you were transferred together from one room to the next?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: No, no. First, when we arrived, we went upstairs. And for a while, we were together. On that night when those guys from Stajicevo came.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, were you in the same room as Mr. Berghofer at any time following this interrogation that you've described to us today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were together in the meantime. But I don't remember that he was in the room when I went outside, when I went out. But before that, he was. We were in the same room, where we could see each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Okay. You say "we were together in the meantime." And then you say, "But before that, he was." I find that answer a bit ambiguous. My question is, and let me broaden it slightly, did you see or speak with Mr. Berghofer after this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: After Hadzic's interrogation, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, not immediately after. But any time between 1991, when you say this interrogation occurred, and the time that you were released, which you now say is April 1992, did you speak to Mr. Berghofer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Before the war. Yes, we said good morning to each other, and we were on greeting terms because we lived only a couple of houses apart. Once he asked me for money, but I wouldn't lend him any. So he was a bit sore at me. But before the war, we were in that Hungarian school together. He was a warehouse keeper. It was before the war. And we arrived at Mitrovica together later on ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My question did not concern before the war, Mr. Pribudic. My question concerned the period after your interrogation and before you were released from Sremska Mitrovica. Did you have occasion to speak with Mr. Berghofer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you tell him about this --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Only I don't know in which room that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you tell him about --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, sorry, Mr. Pribudic. I hear -- I heard two different answers and this could be perhaps a problem with the audio or translation. But did you or did you not speak with Mr. Berghofer after -- any time after this interrogation before your release from Sremska Mitrovica? Weeks later? At any time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: We were not together, and we didn't speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So your testimony is that you never spoke to Dragutin Berghofer between the time of this interrogation and the time of your release, in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: He was not in my room. He was not with me and, therefore, we didn't speak. He was not in room 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I think I will have to take this up after the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, we take the first break for 30 minutes and come back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: While attempts are made to reconnect the videolink, I have a very short oral ruling. On 19 October, the Defence requested a seven-day extension of the deadline for it to respond to the Prosecution's bar table motion. On the same day, the Prosecution indicated that it did not oppose the request. The Trial Chamber hereby grants the request and orders that the Defence response to the Prosecution's bar table motion shall be filed by no later than Thursday, 31st of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Correction for the transcript, the oral ruling. The -- it -- sorry. In the transcript, it is said 19 October, the Defence request, but it should be 16 October. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we have this technical pause, I have a technical matter that I can perhaps take up, use this time with. There was a -- an official final translation of one of the witness's prior statements which came through recently, and we requested the Prosecution this morning to upload the final revised translation. At least my understanding is that that was the request, but I'm not sure yet if it has gone through. Now if I can just say in advance, I have hard copies of the final translation, just in case there is any problem at all with the version in e-court. And the 65 ter number of that is 06487.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Are we ready to proceed, Madam Registrar, in Osijek?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour. We reconnected again and it should be fine now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gosnell, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Maybe I could just ask before we start, so there isn't an interruption as we're going through, as to whether the final version is uploaded and released? If not, it's not a problem. We can just use the hard copy, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I just became aware of its existence this morning, Mr. President. I believe it's come from CLSS. There's probably no problem, but we would like a chance to examine it. Could I suggest that -- I believe it's been uploaded. Perhaps we could just give it a point, a decimal so that it is distinguished, rather than replacing the existing translation that we've been working off of up until this point. I don't know whether counsel intends to offer it at some point, but I suppose we'll wait until we get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I would have no objection to a decimal point to distinguish it from the unrevised version. I also only became aware of the finalised version extremely recently before this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can that be done, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, as long as the uploaded numbers from e-court are communicated to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do we have the uploaded number?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We don't have a Defence -- separate Defence upload number because it was -- my understanding from my side was that it had to be released by the Prosecution. Since it's -- all it is is a -- it's a translation revision of their document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, do you have the 65 ter number in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can the -- can it just be given a Defence 65 ter number? Would that be easier?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We have no problem with that. But it will be a bit strange, won't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm informed that once it's re-uploaded it will be as 65 ter 6457 -- excuse me, 87. Let me just ... 6487.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Will that do, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you. I thank my friends. And thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Pribudic, when you saw Mr. Hadzic on the Vuka bridge two to three years before the war, did he have a beard or was he clean-shaven?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I think he had a beard. Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now you testified that the individuals in the -- in the room referred to him as Goran. Did they use his last name at any time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, before I ask you some more questions about this incident, I want to try to pin down the date of your release from Sremska Mitrovica, and at page 21, line 2, you testified it was from the 7th of April. So from the 20th or 21st up until the 7th of April. And that was your testimony about the period of detention at Sremska Mitrovica. So is that a correct reflection of your memory as to when you were released, the 7th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. The 7th of April, 1992, that's when I was released. I think it was past noon. Two buses took us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How are you able, after all these years, to remember such a specific date? Is there something that allows you to situate the date of your release so specifically?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Well, in all the documents that I have at home, all these papers state that date. Detained at Sremska Mitrovica from/to. That's what the documents state. I cannot forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And yet, at page 16, line 19, you say, in answer to a question of the Prosecutor: "I was released on the 2nd of July." Were you referring to something else when you said that, or were you confused, or is the transcript incorrect, or is there an inconsistency?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to the compound question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's compound in the extreme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, we have the witness's answer. I think he said he didn't say that, and that's the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 06487, please. And I would like for the English to be point 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember, on the 5th of August of this year, you met with the -- some representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, and you were shown a statement from -- that you had given earlier to some Croatian officials. And you gave that earlier statement in April 2010 --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- and you reviewed that statement with them. And then you --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- and then you signed a certification of that statement, in which you said that you recognised the record of interview, even though you had not previously seen it, and you say: "I confirm the accuracy" -- and this is on page 2 of the cover page of the certification. You say: "I confirm the accuracy of this statement. I have been asked whether there are any errors in this statement that need to be corrected or clarified. I have not found any errors, although I do believe that the statement is somewhat abbreviated, may not contain all of the details that I provided to the investigative judge." Now is that right that you signed that certification when you met with the Prosecutor on the 5th of August, 2013?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: No, no. No. No. When it was done, it was thrown onto the desk in front of me, that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps we can turn to page 2 of the B/C/S document on the page in front of us. And hopefully the Registrar in Osijek can locate that. And if we can just turn the page over to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pribudic, can you see your signature there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: That's a statement that I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And am I right that you meant to say that there were -- that you had reviewed your previous statement as was provided to you on that date, and that you found that there were no errors in it, and that it was accurate, subject to saying that it wasn't -- it was somewhat abbreviated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask you to turn over to the -- to the statement itself that you gave in 2010. And please look at the very, very last line there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in English -- the English translation is 06487.2 and it's at page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now what it says there in your statement, which you say is accurate, or which you said was accurate in August 2013, you say: "Finally, I can say that I was exchanged on 27 February 1992." Now, that's different from what you told us, and I understand that. But my question is this: Why, in your previous statement, or how, were you able to be so specific that you thought the date of your exchange was the 27th of February, 1992; whereas today you've told us - again specifically - that's in April 1992, April 7th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: The month of April, yes. It's not correct that I said this, what you just stated. All my documents state the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And between the time of your interrogation with Mr. Hadzic and your release, it's at least three months, if not a little longer; is that right? Sorry, Mr. Pribudic, you don't need to look at your statement for this. And perhaps I don't need to even ask a question. I can just put it to you. According to your testimony now, it was more than three months between the time of your interrogation and your release. So my question is this: You've told us that you discussed your interrogation with Mr. Cakalic. Did you discuss the interrogation by Mr. Hadzic with any of your other fellow inmates?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I didn't talk to anyone. I didn't talk to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, why wouldn't you mention this event to your fellow inmates? I mean, surely this was, for you, a significant and traumatic experience. Well, first of all, is that correct? Do you view this as a traumatic experience?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I was hospitalised twice in Vinkovci in the meantime, and whomever I met of my friends, I told them that I was going to be interviewed by the ICTY investigators. But I didn't speak to anybody about details or anything else. I told them that it was three or four days previously, and then I met people at my gate and I would tell them that they had called me to come and testify, and they all encouraged me. They said, Ljubo, you should go ahead and do it. But I didn't talk to them about any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: While you were detained at Sremska Mitrovica did you know and did you speak with someone named Vilim Karlovic? That name again, Vilim Karlovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: While you were detained at Sremska Mitrovica prison, did you have the acquaintance of anyone there named Vilim Karlovic? Vilim Karlovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Come again?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: While --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: What was the name again?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Vilim Karlovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Vilim Karlovic. Yes, I knew him at Mitrovica. Yes. Yes, he was by me for a while, and then he went to stay by Dragan. He was the room leader. I had seen him at the Vukovar front a year before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you say he was by you for a while, do I understand you to say that he was near you in one of the rooms in which you were detained? In terms of where he was sleeping.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was in the same room as I was, and we shared food. I think that he stayed behind when I left, when I was singled out and left on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you describe to him or recount to him in any way having been interrogated by the man whom you think was Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I -- I didn't talk to him. I saw him once at a petrol station, and we exchanged greetings, and that was all. And my son asked me, Dad, who was that? And I said it was a man who was imprisoned together with me. And that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you know Dragutin Guzovski while you were detained at Sremska Mitrovica, and was he a fellow inmate there? And let me repeat that name, Dragutin Guzovski, G-u-z-o-v-s-k-i.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I'm not hearing this. The headphones are not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me try again. I'm asking you whether you were acquainted at Sremska Mitrovica with anyone named Dragutin Guzovski, G-u-z-o-v-s-k-i and if the answer is --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Dragutin Guzovski, I know him very well. We are very good friends. But I didn't see him at Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you at any time subsequent to your release from Sremska Mitrovica tell Mr. Guzovski about your interrogation by the man whom you think was Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Same question in respect of someone named Zdravko Komsic, K-o-m-c-i -- s-i-c. Did you have his acquaintance at Sremska Mitrovica and --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I know him well, as well. He lives close to my house. But we never discussed this. I was -- I wanted to get in touch with him just now to tell him that I was about to leave for The Hague, but he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, other than Mr. Cakalic, then, can you tell us whether you mentioned this interrogation with the man you believed to be Mr. Hadzic to anyone at all who was a fellow inmate in the months following this event?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I discussed this with Cakalic, and I did speak out loud. I don't know if anybody heard, I don't know, from among the people who were around us. I told this to Cakalic because he was right next to me. And that was just before I dropped to the ground. I didn't speak to anyone else about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now you testified -- or, well, perhaps I should ask you: Is it right that this interrogation occurred in a basement room, according to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. What was it that happened in the basement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was the interrogation that we're discussing today --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Hadzic's slapping?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Yes, indeed, Mr. Pribudic. Where this slapping occurs, did that occur in a basement room?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Hadzic's abuse was in the basement, yes. Now what you have been asking me about had nothing to do with the basement. Because I was taken from the basement to the room where I was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the man who was in that room with the Kalashnikov, was he one of the regular guards at Sremska Mitrovica prison? Did you recognise him as such based on his attire or by recognising him facially?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I had never seen the man. Or perhaps I did see him before, but I didn't know him. He told me, Ljubo, wait until I have my way with you. And I dropped to my knees. And I thought, I'm done for. But who he was, I don't know. He trained his Kalashnikov at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How long did the interrogation last from the time that you walked in the door until the time that you walked out the door?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I wasn't really keeping the time. I wasn't paying attention to that. But not long. Five or six of Hadzic's slaps, and five or six questions. It mustn't have lasted long.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you say it was more or less than five minutes? Are you able to give us any precision at all about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: More than five minutes. Five minutes is nothing. He steps in, asks a question, slaps me, goes out into the next room. My impression was that there was somebody in that room. I heard some whispering there. Then he came back and then asked me, Does -- does Mrkic owe you money? And then goes out again. Comes in again, asking me about my sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how many times, according to you, does Mr. Hadzic come in and out of the room? On how many separate occasions does he enter the room?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Where did I put ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pribudic --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: That's not it. What's this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm not asking you to refer to any notes or document at this stage. I would -- I would ask you -- I would ask you -- I would ask you, first of all --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I don't need them. I don't need them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you what have you written on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: This piece of paper? These are the notes I made this morning. I wanted to write down the order in which Hadzic put his questions to me. And then I came up to number three or four, and that's it. Hadzic came in. He said, You're Pribudic. You're Ljubo. And then he went to the other ones who told him that everything was fine. Then the second question was: Does Mladen owe you money? The third question was: Where is your membership card? Who are you, where do you come from, where are your sons and telling me how he was going to kill them. Who told you to stand up. Because one of the four men there told me to stand up. I couldn't -- my legs couldn't hold me anymore. But that's what I have written down on this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, would you have any objection to handing over those notes to Madam Registrar so that we can keep them or take a copy of them and bring them back to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Give it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Now, I'm not sure you answered my question and it may be a difficult question to answer, but I'll see if you are now able to answer it. If you were to put a number on the number of times that Mr. Hadzic came in and out of the room, are you able to do that? Can you tell us how many times he did that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, well, it's been 20 years, he went in six times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: By that, you mean he entered and left six times. There were six intervals of separate questions by him to you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how many times --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Let's say a minute each, that would make up six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how many times, according to you, did Mr. Hadzic slap you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Do what? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How many times did he slap you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Every time he stepped into the room he slapped me. Except for the last time, when he said, Take him away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he do anything more than slap you? By that, I mean did he commit any other violence towards you, other than slapping you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: He spat at me. He spat at me. Spat. Hit me with his hand and spat at me. Punched me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Swore my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Punched you with his hand?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Struck me with his arm, and as he turned with the blow, he spat at me when I said that I was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he slap you with his open palm or did he slap you with the back of his hand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, the word was "punch."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I think we're dealing with both, and I'll come back to the -- the punch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: When you asked about slapping, that's the other -- the other times he -- the witness has said that he -- that Hadzic slapped him. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm trying to ask generally, about the slaps in general. Because I believe the record is, according to him, that there have been six -- or there were six.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So but -- but perhaps I could be clearer, Mr. Pribudic. Of those slaps that you say you received, were they with the palm of his hand, were they with the back of his hand, or were they some combination?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: As he turned around, he hit me in the head with the palm of his hand. So I said he was slapping me, but he was striking me in the process. Now the first time he slapped me, he -- he then asked me, Which side did I slap you before? And then I showed him the cheek. And then he slapped me on the other cheek, saying, Just to make sure I don't always slap you in the same spot. So they were slaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he ever hit you with a closed fist?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were these slaps all to the head or the face?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Cheek and head. Yes, he would slap me on the forehead and the cheek.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And aside from the slapping and the spitting, any other physical aggression towards you by Mr. Hadzic, the man who you say is Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Nothing. Not a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's, please, now have a look at your statement. And I'll ask you, please, to look at the second-last paragraph of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In English it's on page -- sorry. It might be the third-last in B/C/S. In English it starts at page 3. Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you describe in this paragraph coming into the room. You say and you describe, are describing the men in the room. And you say: "One had the last naming of Stankovic. I think that he was a judge. One wore a black suit and he took my details. One had a Kalashnikov and he was leaning against the window. And there was Slobodan Savic." Let me, first of all, stop there and ask you this: Is it true that there was -- that the man with the Kalashnikov was leaning against a window?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No -- that's not -- Mr. Pribudic, that is not my question.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: Don't know that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My question was: Is it true that he was leaning against a window?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: If he was leaning against the window. Well, how should I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The reason I --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
utterances.text: I saw him standing by the window and holding a Kalashnikov in his hands. But if he was leaning or not, how am I to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how big was this --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO PRIBUDIC
